explain.say: A nut and bolt hold parts together by squeezing them. You push the bolt through holes in both parts and turn a nut onto its thread with a spanner.

faq.q: Why use a spanner on a nut?
faq.a: A spanner is a lever: the long handle multiplies the turning force of your hand, so you can tighten the nut far more than with your fingers.
asks: Why does a longer spanner help?

faq.q: How does a screw thread work?
faq.a: A thread is a sloping ramp wound round a rod. Turning a nut moves it along the ramp, turning a small twist into a large force along the bolt.

faq.q: Why do nuts and bolts hold so tightly?
faq.a: Tightening stretches the bolt a little, and like a spring it pulls back. That pull squeezes the parts together with a force that can be many tonnes in big bolts.

faq.q: Why does a bolt not just unscrew?
faq.a: Friction in the threads and under the nut is bigger than the small turning effect the clamping force makes on the slope. Vibration can overcome it, so lock nuts are used on machines.
A washer spreads the force of the nut over a wider area so it does not dig into the surface, and gives the nut a smooth face to turn on.

facts: A tightened bolt is stretched slightly, and its springiness provides the clamping force.
Most screw threads are right-handed: turn clockwise to tighten.
